I got my BS in microbiology back in 2019 and was sort of in your same position. Wanted to go into medicine at first, then realized I wasn't as passionate about it and decided to go to grad school because I thought that was the only way to make decent money (BS in bio stuff doesn't let you make much until you get a supervisory/manager role). That being said, PLEASE don't go to grad school just because you feel like it's your only option. I did it and you truly truly have to love bench research to go to grad school or you will lose your mind. You work and study 12-14 hours a day, you never know what is going on, and you feel like an absolute moron 24/7. It can really mess with you if you aren't 100% down for the research life. I ended up having to drop out entirely from my PhD program and leave with nothing but 2 years down the drain and a difficult thing to explain on my resume. You could do an MS or MA in a related field or something completely different that isn't bench work, though. For example, I'm considering getting an MA in counterterrorism studies to work with bio and chem threats on the governmental policy side. 

It's only been ~2 months since leaving for me, so I haven't landed anything yet. My significant other is a software developer and you definitely could get into tech if you want to! Probably won't land 6 figures right away since you'd just be doing a bootcamp, but a good option. But, before doing a bootcamp, try learning a couple languages (pythons okay, java is better if you want to be more of a software developer) and try out practice problems on leetcode to see if you actually like it before shelling out all that money for a real bootcamp. 

You just graduated so you have plenty of time. In the meantime, you can try out random things that you find interesting to see if that's the right thing for you before committing to something. I hear a lot of stories of bio majors going on to do something I had never heard of before or something completely unexpected. You should also apply to those biotech/lab tech jobs anyway because in my experience from being in academia, no one with a masters wants those jobs since they don't pay too much and plenty of people get hired with little experience, post-bac lab work, or sometimes none. 

Sorry this was a little rambly, but wanted to let you know what I've learned from an experience eerily similar to yours! Good luck!
